To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the most common reason for accepting permissions is that users want to use the app; (2) users are not aware of the permission system; (3) users are not familiar with the permission system and its terminology; (4) users do not know how to manage permissions; (5) the permission dialog is too complex and difficult to understand.

(1) users make permission-related decisions with runtime dialogs based on the perceived benefits of the app and the trust in the app developer; and (2) users are not able to recall their decisions and the reasons for them after a period of time.

(i) users are generally aware of the permission dialogs and their purpose, and (ii) users are generally able to identify the reason for their decision, but (iii) users do not consider the privacy implications of their decision, and (iv) the most important factors influencing the user's decision were the permission name and the app icon.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether users make better or worse decisions with the runtime permission dialogs compared to previous permission systems.
the following research questions: (i) What are the main reasons for granting or denying a permission?
the following questions: 1) What factors do users consider when making permission decisions?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the main reasons for granting permissions are convenience and the perceived need for an application to function.
users are not aware of the implications of their decisions, and that they are not aware of how they make decisions.
users are still not well served by the current runtime dialog system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the runtime permission dialogs are effective in helping users make decisions about granting permissions.

users are more likely to grant permissions than they are to deny, that they are less likely to deny permissions for apps they have used in the past, that they tend to grant permissions for apps they trust, that they tend not to grant permissions for unknown apps, and that users tend to grant permissions to apps with which they are currently interacting.
users are more likely to grant permissions when the app has a higher rating, the permission is for a more important feature, and they are more familiar with the app and the permission.
The main takeaway from our work is that
users make permission decisions in the moment, and are not able to recall why they decided as they did.
users are not making decisions about the use of their data with the runtime dialogs.
users are more likely to deny permissions when they do not understand the app's request.
